shm-intro-s1.title: Force on a glider from a spring
shm-intro-s1.text: A 0.40 kg glider on a level air track is attached to a spring. A student holds the glider at several positions and reads the force the spring exerts on it with a force sensor. Position is measured from where the spring is relaxed; + is to the right.

table.caption: Spring force on the glider at each position

shm-intro-s2.title: A pendulum at three points
shm-intro-s2.html: The bob is released from rest at X and swings through Y to Z and back. Air resistance is negligible.

items.q: Which feature of the data shows that the glider, once released, will move in simple harmonic motion?
options: The force is proportional to the displacement and points the opposite way
The force is zero at the position where the spring is relaxed
The force keeps getting more negative as the glider is moved farther to the right
The force has the same size at equal distances on either side

why.correct: SHM needs a restoring force proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and opposite to it: F = −kx. Doubling x doubles F, and the sign is always opposite to x.
options: Right: this is the definition of the restoring force in SHM, F = −kx.
A zero force at equilibrium is true of any oscillation; it does not show the force grows in proportion to the displacement.

True of the data, but it says nothing about proportion or about the left side: a force that pointed left everywhere would never pull the glider back from the left. SHM needs F proportional to x and opposite to it.
Symmetry alone allows forces that are not proportional to x (for example a force that grows as x²).

items.q: What is the spring constant of the spring? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you divided the displacement by the force. The spring constant is force per unit displacement, k = |F|/|x|.
Value: you multiplied force by displacement. k = |F|/|x| = 2.4 N / 0.10 m.

why.correct: From any row, k = |F|/|x| = 2.4 N / 0.10 m = 24 N/m. Every row gives the same value, which is what makes the force proportional to x.

items.q: The glider is pulled to x = +0.080 m and released. What is its acceleration at the moment of release? Take + to the right, include the sign, and give the unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the spring force in newtons. Newton's second law gives a = F/m: divide by the 0.40 kg mass.
Value: the size is right but the direction is wrong. At x = +0.080 m the spring pulls the glider back toward x = 0, so a is negative.

why.correct: F = −kx = −(24 N/m)(0.080 m) = −1.92 N. a = F/m = −1.92 N / 0.40 kg = −4.8 m/s², toward equilibrium.

items.q: When the oscillating glider passes x = 0 moving to the right, what is the net force on it?
options: Zero, even though the glider is moving fast
To the right, in the direction it is moving
To the left, because it will soon turn around
Its largest value, because its speed is largest

why.correct: At x = 0 the spring is relaxed, so the spring force is zero; gravity and the normal force cancel on the level track. Zero net force means zero acceleration at that instant, not zero velocity.
options: Right: x = 0 is the equilibrium position, where the net force is zero.
This is the "a force is needed to keep it moving" idea. The glider keeps moving at x = 0 with no net force at that instant.
The force points left only once the glider is to the right of x = 0 and the spring is stretched.
This mixes up force with speed. The force depends on the displacement, which is zero here.

items.q: Which point is the equilibrium position of the pendulum, and why?
options: Y, where nothing pushes the bob along its path
X, where the bob is momentarily at rest
Z, where the bob stops before turning back
Y, because the bob is moving fastest at that point

why.correct: At Y the string pulls straight up and Earth pulls straight down, so no force acts along the arc. That is the equilibrium position: the bob would stay there if placed at rest.
options: Right: at the equilibrium position the restoring force along the path is zero.
Being at rest for an instant does not make a point the equilibrium position. At X a restoring force pulls the bob back toward Y.
At Z the restoring force is largest, which is the opposite of equilibrium.
Y is the right point, but speed does not define equilibrium; the zero restoring force does.

items.q: What is the amplitude of the pendulum's motion, measured as an angle?

why.correct: Amplitude is the largest displacement from equilibrium, measured from Y. The bob reaches 8° on each side.
options: Right: from Y to X (or to Z) is 8°.
This is the angle from one extreme to the other, which is twice the amplitude.
This halves the amplitude; the bob reaches the full 8° on each side.
The amplitude is not the displacement at equilibrium; it is the largest displacement.

items.q: Why is this pendulum a good example of simple harmonic motion?
options: At small angles the restoring force along the arc is close to proportional to the bob's displacement
The string pulls the bob toward the pivot with a force that stays the same at each point
The bob's weight pulls it down, and gravity is a force that is the same everywhere
The bob moves along a curved path, so it returns to its starting point each cycle

why.correct: Along the arc, gravity has a part of size mg sin θ pointing back toward Y. For small angles sin θ ≈ θ (in radians), so the restoring force is close to mgθ = (mg/ℓ)s, proportional to the displacement s along the arc.
options: Right: a restoring force proportional to the displacement is what SHM needs.
The string force is not constant (it is largest at Y) and it points along the string, not along the path, so it is not the restoring force.
A constant downward force alone does not give a force proportional to the displacement along the arc.
Returning to the start shows periodic motion, not simple harmonic motion.

items.q: The same pendulum is released from 60° instead. Which statement is best?
options: The motion is periodic but noticeably less like SHM, because sin 60° is well below 60° in radians
The motion is still SHM, because a pendulum oscillates about Y at any angle
The motion is no longer periodic, because the bob speeds up too much at Y
The motion is closer to SHM, because a larger angle gives a larger restoring force

why.correct: 60° is 1.05 rad but sin 60° = 0.87, so the restoring force (mg sin θ) is 17% smaller than a force proportional to θ would be. The bob still swings back and forth, but the motion is no longer a close match to SHM.
options: Right: the small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ θ breaks down at large angles.
Oscillating about Y makes the motion periodic; SHM also needs the restoring force to be proportional to the displacement.
Without friction the bob repeats the same swing, so the motion is still periodic.
A larger force is not the test; the force must stay proportional to the displacement, and at 60° it falls short.

items.q: An object moves back and forth along the x-axis about x = 0. Which force on it, written as a function of its position x, gives simple harmonic motion?
options: F = −(6.0 N/m²)x²

why.correct: SHM needs F = −kx: proportional to x and opposite to it. Here k = 6.0 N/m.
options: Right: proportional to the displacement and opposite to it.
This force points away from x = 0, so it pushes the object farther away; there is no oscillation.
This force is proportional to x², not x, and it points in −x on both sides, so it does not restore from the left.
A constant force does not depend on position at all, so it cannot pull back from both sides.

items.q: A ball bounces straight up and down on a hard floor, rising to the same height each time. Why is this periodic motion but not simple harmonic motion?
options: In the air the force on it is its constant weight, not a force proportional to its distance from a center
The ball is not attached to a spring, so there is no restoring force acting on it at any point of its motion
The ball does not return to the same height, so the motion does not repeat
The ball moves fastest at the top, so its speed pattern is reversed

why.correct: Between bounces the only force is the ball's weight, mg downward, which does not change with height. SHM needs a restoring force that grows in proportion to the displacement from equilibrium.
options: Right: a constant force is not a restoring force proportional to displacement.
A pendulum is SHM with no spring; what matters is the form of the restoring force.
The stem says the ball rises to the same height each time, so the motion does repeat.
The ball is slowest at the top, not fastest.

items.q: A block on a spring slides back and forth on a frictionless table. A meterstick beside it shows that its front edge moves between the 0.12 m mark and the 0.38 m mark. What is the amplitude of the motion? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the distance from one turning point to the other, which is twice the amplitude. Amplitude is measured from the middle.
Value: that is a meterstick reading, not a displacement from equilibrium. Equilibrium is halfway, at 0.25 m.

why.correct: Equilibrium is halfway between the turning points, at 0.25 m. The amplitude is the largest displacement from there: 0.38 m − 0.25 m = 0.13 m.

items.q: A 0.50 kg block hangs at rest from a vertical spring with spring constant 40 N/m. How far is the spring stretched from its relaxed length at the block's equilibrium position? Use g = 9.8 m/s². Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you divided the mass by k. The spring must balance the weight, mg = 4.9 N, so stretch = mg/k.

why.correct: At equilibrium the net force is zero: kΔx = mg, so Δx = mg/k = (0.50 kg)(9.8 m/s²)/(40 N/m) = 0.1225 m ≈ 0.12 m. For a hanging spring the equilibrium position is this stretched point, not the relaxed length.

items.q: The block hanging from the vertical spring is pulled down and released. When it is at its lowest point, what is the direction of the net force on it?
options: Upward, toward the equilibrium position
Downward, because its weight pulls down
Zero, because it is momentarily at rest
Downward, in the direction it was moving

why.correct: Below equilibrium the spring is stretched more than at equilibrium, so its upward pull is larger than the weight. The net force points up, toward equilibrium, as a restoring force should.
options: Right: the spring force exceeds the weight below equilibrium.
The weight is there, but the spring's upward pull is larger at the lowest point.
At rest for an instant does not mean zero net force; this is where the net force is largest.
The net force does not follow the motion; it follows the displacement, pointing back toward equilibrium.

items.q: A cart on a horizontal spring oscillates between x = −A and x = +A. Where is the size of its acceleration greatest?
options: At x = −A and x = +A
At x = 0
At x = −A/2 and x = +A/2
The same size at each position along the track

why.correct: The net force is −kx, so its size is largest where |x| is largest, at the turning points. By Newton's second law the acceleration is largest there too, even though the speed is zero.
options: Right: largest displacement, largest restoring force, largest acceleration.
At x = 0 the net force is zero, so the acceleration is zero; this is where the speed is greatest.
The force at ±A/2 is half its value at ±A.
A constant acceleration would need a constant force; the spring force changes with x.

items.q: A block on a horizontal spring is pulled 0.10 m from equilibrium and released. In a second trial the same block on the same spring is pulled 0.20 m. Predict how each quantity in the second trial compares with the first.

variables.name: Size of the spring force at the moment of release
variables.why: F = kx and x doubled, so the force at release doubles.

variables.name: Size of the acceleration at the moment of release
variables.why: a = F/m: twice the force on the same mass gives twice the acceleration.

variables.name: Spring constant
variables.why: k is a property of the spring; pulling it farther does not change it.

why.correct: The restoring force is proportional to the displacement, F = −kx; the spring constant belongs to the spring.

items.q: A spring is replaced by one with twice the spring constant. At the same displacement from equilibrium, how does the restoring force on the block compare?
options: It is twice as large
It is half as large
It is four times as large
It is the same

why.correct: F = −kx: at the same x, doubling k doubles the force.
options: Right: F is proportional to k at a fixed displacement.
A stiffer spring pulls harder, not more gently.
F depends on k to the first power, not k².
The force depends on k as well as x.
